newsitem.title: DUBAI: Arabian Shield gets Saudi mine licence.
newsitem.headline: Arabian Shield gets Saudi mine licence.

text.p: Arabian Shield Development Co (ASDC) has secured a licence to tap a mineral deposit in Saudi Arabia and is negotiating a loan for half the $88 million cost, its president and chief executive said on Sunday.

Hatem al-Khalidi said ASDC was granted the licence in the first week of December for a 50-50 joint venture between ASDC and Saudi partners -- the Saudi Company for Mining Industries -- to mine the deposits. He said negotiations were underway for a loan with the Saudi Industrial Development Fund (SIDF).
"The licence makes the joint venture eligible for an SIDF loan of 50 percent of the total cost of the project of $88 million," he told Reuters by telephone from Jeddah.

ASDC had originally hoped to start production in late 1997, but Khalidi said that was now unfeasible as the SIDF had insisted on an industrial licence before negotiating the loan needed to develop the mine.
"Now we expect production to start 18 months after the financing is secured," he said.
Once the SIDF loan is secured, ASDC would approach Saudi banks for $19 million and start raising the rest of the cost from Saudi investors.
The Nasdaq-listed company has a mining lease for the al-Masane copper, zinc, gold and silver deposit in southwest Saudi Arabia. The lease is for 30 years which could be extended for another 20 years.

The deposit, with proven reserves for 11 years, is expected to produce an annual 58,000 tonnes of zinc concentrates with 54 percent zinc per tonne and 35,000 tonnes of copper concentrates with 25 percent copper. It also expects output of 22,000 ounces of gold and 800,000 ounces of silver per year.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer and exporter, is embarking on a drive to encourage investments in the minerals sector to diversify from oil.

Analysts in the kingdom say slow government approvals for exploration licences is holding back development of the sector, which is forecast to grow faster than any other in the state's five-year plan to 2000, at an average annual real rate of nine percent.
Saudi Arabia already mines eight tonnes of gold a year, but its wealth of zinc, copper, bauxite, phosphates, silver, iron and more gold are waiting to be exploited.
